item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] What next for the ICC and the Palestine investigation after Karim Khan's removal?
item.description:
What next for the ICC and the Palestine investigation after Karim Khan's removal?

Submitted by Sondos Asem on Sat, 07/25/2026 - 11:16
The court's removal of the chief prosecutor leaves it with a stalled Palestine file, two sanctioned deputies in charge, and facing an election to choose Khan's successor
Then International Criminal Court (ICC) chief prosecutor Karim Khan in The Hague, Netherlands, 16 January 2025 (Reuters/Piroschka van de Wouw/File Photo)
Off

Member states of the International Criminal Court voted on Friday to remove chief prosecutor Karim Khan over misconduct claims, with 82 of the court's 125 members backing dismissal in a secret ballot at the United Nations in New York.

It is the first time in the court's 24-year history that a sitting prosecutor has been removed, and it caps an 18-month disciplinary process that Palestinian rights groups, former judges and the prosecutor's lawyers have described as politicised. Khan has denied any wrongdoing.

The vote has opened several questions on the fate of the Palestine investigation and who will be elected to be his predecessor. 

In particular, Khan's departure and Israel's official reaction have prompted questions as to whether it will have any impact on the arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant, which were issued during Khan’s leadership.

Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar described Khan's removal as "long-delayed", calling on the court to drop the arrest warrants "immediately", reiterating Israel's debunked claim that it was rushed to distract from sexual misconduct allegations. 

So, what now?

What happens to Khan?

The removal decision takes immediate effect, according to the court’s rules. Khan is no longer a member of the court and has been removed from every case in the office's portfolio, including Palestine.

His lawyers on Friday said that Khan would challenge "the lawfulness and fairness of the decision through all available legal mechanisms".

Khan told Middle East Eye in May that he would take any dismissal to the International Labour Organization Administrative Tribunal (ILOAT), the forum where ICC staff contest employment decisions.

The Karim Khan saga: a timeline
Read More »

His central argument against the decision would likely be that a panel of three judicial experts appointed by the executive body of the Assembly of States Parties, the bureau, itself concluded unanimously in March that the UN investigators' findings on the allegations "do not establish misconduct or breach of duty under the relevant framework", a conclusion the bureau voted to set aside.

MEE also revealed this month that the bureau changed the voting rules, merging a two-stage vote into a single motion and lowering the effective threshold for removal. That is another procedural issue that may be brought before the tribunal. 

Abdul Koroma, a former judge of the International Court of Justice, has said the prospects of a successful appeal are "considerable".

But an ILOAT challenge is untested terrain.

As ICC scholars Ezequiel Jimenez and Sergey Vasiliev have noted, ILOAT case law is "calibrated to labour relations within international organisations", and it is "far from settled" whether a political decision by a plenary treaty body to remove an elected official falls within its jurisdiction.

Even a favourable award may not translate into reinstatement. By the time ILOAT rules, a successor may already be in post. Proceedings typically take years.

Will US sanctions on Khan be lifted?

This remains uncertain. Nothing in the executive order provides for automatic removal on leaving office, and the current administration has shown no indication that it intends to lift the sanctions.

The US State Department has not responded to a request from MEE for comment on the matter.

Khan was the first person designated under Executive Order 14203, signed by President Donald Trump in February 2025 in retaliation for the Netanyahu and Gallant warrants. His assets were blocked, his US visa revoked and his family barred from entry.

But there is a precedent for delisting. Although Khan's predecessor, Fatou Bensouda, was sanctioned in September 2020 over the Afghanistan investigation, those sanctions were lifted in April 2021, when the Biden administration revoked the order outright. But Bensouda was still in office at the time, with her term running until June 2021. 

Her delisting, therefore, followed a change of US administration and policy, not her departure from the court.

What happens to the Palestine investigation?

Following the removal vote, the ICC’s office of the prosecutor released a statement saying that its work would continue without interruption. In addition to the Palestine investigation, the court has more than a dozen active situations, including Ukraine, Darfur, Libya and Afghanistan.

MEE has exclusively reported that the office in April sought an arrest warrant application for Israel’s Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, and that another application for National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir was being prepared.

Khan’s departure may impact how the office prioritises applications or resists external pressures and sanctions. MEE last year reported that the Smotrich and Ben Gvir applications, for example, were ready before Khan went on leave in May 2025, but were shelved for months as the interim prosecutors, as well as the court itself, were under threat of sanctions. 

Exclusive: ICC prosecutor's office seeks arrest warrant for Israel's Smotrich
Read More »

Khan played a key role in indicting Israeli leaders after a turbulent 15-year process in which his two predecessors failed to apply for any warrants for Israelis. After his election in 2021, he prioritised the Palestine investigation and dedicated additional resources to it.

However, the warrants issued for Netanyahu and Gallant on 21 November 2024 remain in force, and should not be immediately impacted by Khan’s departure. Only judges can withdraw them, and they have repeatedly declined to.

Since the warrants were issued, Israel has mounted a series of legal challenges aimed at getting them thrown out. Two are still pending. 

The most consequential is Israel's argument that the court has no jurisdiction over its nationals at all, since Israel isn’t a state party to the Rome Statute.

In April 2025, the Appeals Chamber ruled that the lower chamber had wrongly brushed this aside as premature, and sent it back to be decided properly.

More than a year on, that decision has still not come, and whichever way it goes, it will almost certainly be appealed again, pushing a final answer well into 2027.

The second is a request filed in November 2025 to disqualify Khan for alleged bias and cancel the warrants he obtained. The call for disqualification falls away now that he has been removed.

But whether Israel presses the wider claim, that warrants sought by a prosecutor since found guilty of serious misconduct are themselves tainted, is an open question, and one Israeli officials have already begun to trail publicly.

The rest have failed. In December 2025, the Appeals Chamber rejected Israel's claim that referrals filed by seven states after 7 October 2023 amounted to a new investigation, requiring the prosecutor to notify Israel afresh and give it a chance to investigate its own officials instead.

The judges held that events after 7 October were already covered by the notice issued in 2021. Had Israel won, the warrants would have fallen and the process would have had to start again.

In July 2025, judges refused Israel's request to suspend the warrants and freeze the wider investigation while the jurisdiction question is resolved, ruling that they stand until that question is answered.

Who runs the office of the prosecutor now?

The office of the prosecutor said on Friday that it "takes note" of the decision to remove Khan, and confirmed that deputy prosecutors Nazhat Shameem Khan, of Fiji, and Mame Mandiaye Niang, of Senegal, "will continue to head the office", as they have done since Khan took leave in May 2025.

Both deputies were also sanctioned by the US in August 2025 for maintaining the Netanyahu and Gallant warrants after assuming leadership of the office.

Neither is an acting prosecutor. The office is being run by two deputies, not by an interim officeholder, and it has now been without an elected head for more than a year.

What's the timeline for electing a new prosecutor?

Removal triggers a fresh election under Article 42 of the Rome Statute, the fourth in the court's history. The prosecutor is elected by secret ballot for a nine-year term by an absolute majority of state parties.

The 25th session of the Assembly of States Parties runs from 7 to 17 December 2026 at the UN headquarters in New York, a session which will also include the election of six judges. 

'Nothing bars either sitting deputy [Nazhat Shameem Khan or Mame Mandiaye Niang] from being nominated by a state party'

- Ezequiel Jimenez, ICC expert

Given how long the office has gone without an elected head, Ezequiel Jimenez argued the election should happen as soon as possible, even by the December session of the Assembly or a resumed session in early 2027.  

A new bureau also takes office in December, which will help shape how the process is run.

It’s unclear, however, whether an election this year or early next year is feasible. Little more than four months separate Khan's removal from the December session.

The last election took 22 months from the bureau adopting the terms of reference in April 2019 to the vote that chose Khan in February 2021. Bensouda was the sitting deputy prosecutor when she was elected, and it still took about a year.

Concerning term length, court rules set a nine-year, non-renewable term "unless a shorter term is decided upon at the time of their election". That gives state parties the option to elect a successor for the remainder of Khan's term (roughly four years) to June 2030, rather than for a full nine.

Jimenez suggested that the assembly could go further and narrow the field to the two sitting deputy prosecutors, granting the winner the balance of the term to secure a swift result. That would require consensus, and any state party can nominate its own candidate.

The 2020 contest that produced Khan deviated from the pathway the assembly had agreed, with states abandoning the vetted shortlist produced by the Committee on the Election of the Prosecutor.

Bensouda, by contrast, was elected by consensus in 2011. 

“Nothing bars either sitting deputy [Nazhat Shameem Khan or Mame Mandiaye Niang] from being nominated by a state party,” Jimenez told MEE.

He added that gender balance and regional rotation might play a role. The post has gone to Latin America (Luis Moreno Ocampo), Africa (Bensouda) and Western Europe (Khan). Asia Pacific and Eastern Europe have never held it. 

“Will western Europe ask for their 'turn' again? Or will it be someone from Asia or Eastern Europe? These factors will be part of the new election,” Jimenez added.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] 'We want to see blood': Israeli political leadership and settler groups call for revenge against Palestinians
item.description:
'We want to see blood': Israeli political leadership and settler groups call for revenge against Palestinians

Submitted by Nadav Rapaport on Sat, 07/25/2026 - 14:37
Rights groups and Palestinian officials report homes burned, civilians injured and arrests following deadly clashes near Nablus
Palestinians walk through smoke from a fire near the village of Tell, west of Nablus in the occupied West Bank, after a reported settler attack, 18 July 2026 (Jaafar Ashtiyeh/AFP)
Off

Israeli political leaders and settler organisations have called for "revenge" against Palestinians, saying they "want to see blood" and "erase the village of Tell". 

Israel's finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, on Friday called for the destruction of the villages of Tell, Iraq Burin and Beit Furik, stating that these communities "should look exactly like the refugee camps in Nablus and Tulkarm", referring to the large-scale destruction the Israeli military has inflicted there.

"The population there needs to be evacuated," Smotrich added, calling on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to strip the area from the Palestinian Authority's responsibility.

Israel's national security minister, Itamar Ben Gvir, said that "for every Jew killed, the enemy must bear the loss of land and homes", calling for the adoption of Israel's strategy of razing entire cities in the Gaza Strip in the West Bank as well.

The calls come after armed Israeli settlers, escorted by the military, raided the Palestinian village of Tell amid surging settler violence in the occupied West Bank. 

Four members of the Saifi family were killed by Israeli fire, after the Israeli military claimed one of them seized a weapon from a settler, subsequently shooting the settler to death.

According to the Palestinian health ministry, at least 87 Palestinians have been killed in the territory in 2026 by Israeli fire, including 21 killed by settlers.

Zvi Sukkot, a member of Smotrich's Religious Zionism party, also called for destruction, telling Channel 14 News on Friday that the village of Tell "needs to become ruins", while on the same day posting on his Facebook page a black screen with the caption: "Revenge."

Israeli settler militia, Hilltop Youth, echoed the call. 

Messages reviewed by Middle East Eye from a settler group chat included appeals to "erase the village of Tell" shortly after news of the killings emerged. 

"We want revenge. Not settlements, not promises of more housing units," one message read.

"We want to see blood. There is no comfort without revenge," the message read, with an attached picture of a river of blood.

Elchanan Groner, a prominent hilltop settler, said that "the village of murderers, Tell, must be erased now", while in a tribute to the hilltop settler who died, Groner wished "to avenge your pure blood".

'Settle the score' 

Netanyahu said on his X account that "we will pursue terror everywhere," adding that Israel "will settle accounts with them".

The prime minister added that he instructed the Israeli military to demolish the family home of the Palestinian man who killed the settler and to act swiftly and powerfully against other villages in the area. 

Israeli settlers rampage through Palestinian village near Nablus
Read More »

Netanyahu also said that he had ordered the acceleration of regularisation and establishment of more settler outposts, from which many settler attacks - including the one in Tell - originated.

In response to the clashes, which Israel is defining as a terror attack, Haaretz reported on Friday that the Israeli army mobilised troops in the West Bank for a large-scale operation around Nablus in the northern part of the Palestinian territory.

According to a report by the Palestinian news agency Wafa, the Israeli army has so far arrested 66 Palestinians across the West Bank, including 30 Palestinian civilians who were detained in Tell.

The military closed the entrances to Tell and to the nearby Burin village, while fully encircling the city of Nablus, Haaretz reported on Saturday morning.

The Israeli army reportedly raided Palestinian homes in different communities in the West Bank, detaining civilians and conducting searches, with Palestinian reports indicating military vandalism.

The Israeli army also raided a hospital in Nablus, Quds News Network reported on Friday, with the military saying they arrested two Palestinians who were involved in the violent clashes in Tell earlier that day.

Settler attacks

Meanwhile, settlers raided Palestinian communities across the West Bank as well, after Israeli leaders and settler organisers called for revenge against Palestinians.

The Palestine Red Crescent Society (PRCS) reported on Friday that eight Palestinians had been injured, including one in critical condition, during a settler attack on the village of Far'ata near Qalqilya, with Palestinians saying settlers set homes on fire and threw stones. 

Israeli settlers kill four Palestinians in West Bank attack
Read More »

In addition, the PRCS said that three other Palestinians were injured on Friday during a settler raid on the town of Sarra, near Nablus, with Palestinian reports saying settlers set homes on fire and damaged Palestinian property in the town.

Quds News Network reported on violent settler attacks at additional locations, including in Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron, and in the villages of Awarta and Urif, near Nablus, where settlers reportedly set fire to property and uprooted olive trees.

Quds News Network also reported that in the town of Qarawat Bani Hassan, near Salfit, settlers seized a home and raised the Israeli flag over it.

Wafa news agency reported on similar attacks by settlers on the village of Birin, east of Hebron, the village of Abu Njeim, southeast of Bethlehem, and on Kafr Malik's water infrastructure in the Ramallah governorate.

Haaretz reported on more settler attacks on the villages of Jit, Iraq Burin, and Tell in the Nablus area, while settlers reportedly stabbed and injured a Palestinian man in Wadi al-Mu'arrajat in the Jordan Valley.

The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, has requested the armed forces to deploy an Airbus A400M military transport aircraft earlier than originally planned to help tackle the major wildfires in Gironde, according to Le Monde.

The French newspaper reported the aircraft’s use was not originally expected until the end of the month due to the technical preparations and tests required beforehand.

While the fires raging across forests in France are a dramatic reminder of three successive heatwaves in as many months, the state of the country’s rivers provides another, no less worrying insight into the impact of extreme heat supercharged by the climate crisis.

The Loire, France’s longest river, is at a historical low, with the flow of some branches, including through the city of Orléans, reduced to a trickle between sandbanks. Two weeks ago, 16% of French rivers were reported to have dried up. A quarter of small streams were stagnant or had disappeared altogether, according to the national low water observatory. There has been little rain since.

US President Donald Trump has, for now, set aside plans to sharply escalate the American military campaign against Iran, with growing concern that a wider war could dangerously deplete the Pentagon's stockpile of Patriot missile interceptors and other air defence munitions in the Middle East, The New York Times reports.

According to the newspaper, Trump discussed the conflict with senior advisers and cabinet officials during a meeting on Friday.

The New York Times said Gen Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, has privately warned that while renewed large-scale operations against Iran are militarily feasible, they would dangerously reduce interceptor stocks available to US Central Command, which oversees operations across the Middle East.

The risks of resuming major combat operations, including the prospect of a broader regional war, the vulnerability of Gulf allies to Iranian attacks, and the potential for global economic disruption were also discussed.
